chapter: Joining Raeburn and work for other leaders
title: Rejoining Boyd Raeburn and the breakthrough on 'There's No You'
summary: Returning when Harry Biss was hurt, writing 'There's No You' he felt all limits fall away.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: (Johnny) Bothwell had had an argument with probably the rest of the band, because he was quite a character and Boyd finally told him he'd have to go and he called McKusick who was living with me, and Hal went and rejoined them, because he had been with them until I pulled him out of the band to come to the coast with me.
To work at Paramount at the studios?
I told him that I could find him work if he came out there with me.

He rejoined them in San Francisco and a few weeks later they called me--Harry Biss who had been playing with them blew his top one night and put his fist through a glass door and cut his arm up so he couldn't play, and that's when it happened. I went back and rejoined the

band and he wanted a chart on "There's No You" and I sat down and I can't tell you what happened but there was a click in my life, something clicked, all the fences went down and I could see, my horizon was limitless, I could write anything I wanted anytime.

As I said, down went the fences and I don't know what else could have been involved in the sudden understanding. I think a great deal of it was my anger at how I had been treated by everyone, the world, people who were supposedly close to me, my loves, my friends; I felt somehow as if I had been brutalized and I resented everything. I resented people telling me you can't do this, you can't do it, it isn't done, people won't understand and I just suddenly said, I can do anything. If I do it it's right; if you don't like it, that's opinion, and they have a right to their opinion, but they do not have the right to tell me I can't do it.
Were you aware of this revelation while you were writing that or
No, it was there before I put the first mark on paper.
Was that a particularly good tune, did you like that tune? Was that helpful?
It was a fine tune, but it wouldn't have mattered what the tune was. I was just ready at that moment; that was the time. That was it, and it was unbelievably easy, to just go on and do it.
Where did you write that, were you in a hotel room?
Right. I was at the Palace Hotel in San Francisco.
From that point on, everything. We're a little out of order, but I'll continue it. Tell me about when you brought the chart down--
